newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan urged to push APEC economics, not politics.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan urged to push APEC economics, not politics.

text.p: World number three in foreign exchange reserves, aggressive Asian investor, export juggernaut even in slow years, respected military power, fledgling democracy. Taiwan is all of these and more.
Yet, as in each of the past three years, rival China is barring Taiwan's leader from this year's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the Philippines.

Taipei analysts say it is unfair that Taiwan, which has made or promised many free-trade concessions, is seeing its rights in APEC and other world economic bodies constrained by political objections from Beijing.
But they also urge Taiwan to put aside political arguments and flex its massive economic muscle to improve its already substantial ties with foreign countries.
"Politics is Taiwan's weakest point and there's no way we can avoid political influence in economic activities," said Wu Hui-lin of Taipei's independent Chung-hua Institute for Economic Research.

China has seen Taiwan as a rebel province since a civil war split them in 1949 and, in its quest to bring the island under its influence, demands that Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui not be accorded the status of a national leader at international or bilateral gatherings.
The APEC summit in Subic Bay is no exception.
The Philippines, rejecting Taiwan's pleas not to be swayed by China's political agenda, refused to invite President Lee or Premier Lien Chan to the leadership summit.

China tolerates Taiwan's APEC membership not as a sovereign but as a customs territory, and Taiwan's summit seat will be filled for the second year by tycoon Koo Chen-fu -- Taipei's top China negotiator and a senior adviser to the president.
Taiwan's 49-strong ministerial team led by cabinet economic planning chief Chiang Ping-kun and economics minister Wang Chih-kang left for Manila on Wednesday.
Under pressure from China, President Lee missed the past three APEC summits in Seattle in 1993, Bogor, Indonesia, in 1994 and Osaka in 1995.
"We should forget about politics and make the world focus on Taiwan's economic power," analyst Wu said. "For many countries, they need Taiwan for economic reasons."
Taiwan's foreign exchange reserves were US$86.678 billion at the end of September, eclipsed only by Japan's and China's.

Despite political isolation imposed by China, the island is one of the top investors in Asia, pouring tens of millions of dollars into Southeast Asia, partially as a result of government appeals not to invest too heavily in the Chinese mainland.
In 1995, Taiwan's trade with Asia totalled US$110 billion.
"No country can deny the fact that Taiwan is very important economically in this region," said Ray Tung, a director of the independent Taiwan Institute of Economic Research.
"Taiwan can play a very active role and introduce its experience of transforming into an industrialised country from an agriculture state," Tung said.

Taiwan's experience helping thousands of small and medium enterprises at home and abroad and its huge overseas investments also are powerful levers to woo support at APEC and other economic forums, analysts said.
"It's not important who will go to the APEC summit. It's more important to tell other countries how they can benefit from (relations with) Taiwan," Wu said.
